selection_basis: Three purposively selected historical letters with concrete communication purposes, before any experimental model output. Not a random sample or a held-out corpus.
origin: Existing official PG mirror acquired on Furnace in August 2026, subsequently cold-stored; three members read without modifying the archive or training data.
human_ledger_review: pending; assistant-drafted acceptable readings are not an independent gold standard
reuse_status: Local inspection/preparation only. Keep full cached PG headers/licenses locally. Publication and provider-processing review remain pending; catalog/ebook US notices do not establish worldwide clearance.
scan_status: Cached transcriptions inspected; original printed pages not visually compared. Score relative to the frozen transcription, not an asserted autograph transcription.

cases.author: Jane Austen
cases.edition: The Letters of Jane Austen; selected by Sarah Chauncey Woolsey from the Brabourne compilation; Little, Brown, Boston, 1908. Ebook credits Suzanne Shell, Emmy and Distributed Proofreaders; updated 2024-10-23.
cases.locator: Letter V, Rowling, Sunday (September 18), opening two paragraphs. Heading does not state a year.
cases.purpose: Explain a contingent travel arrangement and the reply needed before proceeding.
cases.omitted_context: Later family news, a hoped-for pickup, reflections on the earlier plan, and a humorous postscript are excluded. The opening reverses the captain/ship names; do not silently correct it or test their real-world identities.

probes.question: When does Frank need to be in town, and why has he delayed leaving?
probes.acceptable_reading: Wednesday; he remains until then to accommodate the writer, rather than leaving on the earlier intended day.
evidence: be in town on Wednesday
He remains till Wednesday merely to accommodate me.
probes.loss_to_watch: Conflating the earlier intended departure with the current Wednesday arrangement.

probes.question: What communication is the writer waiting for, and when does she expect to know its result?
probes.acceptable_reading: A reply from Miss P. about receiving her on Wednesday; she wrote again requesting return of post and expects to know on Tuesday. This is an expectation, not a received confirmation.
evidence: I have written to her again to-day, and desired her to answer it by return of post.
On Tuesday, therefore, I shall positively know whether they can receive me on Wednesday.
probes.loss_to_watch: Turning an expected reply into an already confirmed invitation.

probes.question: What alternative travel arrangement is described, and what conditions govern it?
probes.acceptable_reading: If they cannot receive her on Wednesday, Edward has promised to take her to Greenwich the following Monday, if that suits them better; this is not an unconditional confirmed journey.
evidence: If they cannot, Edward has been so good as to promise to take me to Greenwich on the Monday following
if that suits them better.
probes.loss_to_watch: Keeping Monday and Edward but deleting the conditions.

probes.question: What will the writer do if no answer arrives by the stated deadline?
probes.acceptable_reading: If none arrives on Tuesday, she must suppose Mary is away and wait until she hears. This is an inference and a waiting policy, not proof of Mary's absence or permission to leave anyway.
evidence: If I have no answer at all on Tuesday, I must suppose Mary is not at home, and must wait till I do hear
probes.loss_to_watch: Collapsing no reply into a negative reply or a known absence.

probes.question: Does the excerpt establish whether the Pearsons are actually at home?
probes.acceptable_reading: No; their availability remains unresolved in this excerpt. Do not infer absence from lack of a reply.
evidence: I cannot go on the uncertainty of the Pearsons being at home

cases.author: Charles Darwin
cases.recipient: John Murray; identified by the preceding editorial introduction, not inserted into the message
cases.edition: Life and Letters of Charles Darwin, Volume 2; edited by Francis Darwin. Cached ebook credits Sue Asscher and David Widger; updated 2022-01-15. Exact underlying print edition not established by the cached title page.
cases.locator: Chapter 2.X; Down, September 21 [1861], letter introduced as addressed to Mr. Murray, ending immediately before the September 24 letter.
cases.purpose: Ask for candid publication advice, state doubts, and specify a financial boundary.
cases.end_anchor: cares for the success of a book.
cases.omitted_context: Preceding editorial context and subsequent acceptance/offer correspondence are excluded. The printed ellipsis inside the selected letter is inherited from this edition, not a new deletion. Do not reconstruct omitted material or later outcomes.

probes.question: What decision does the writer ask the recipient to advise on, and how should that advice be given?
probes.acceptable_reading: Whether to publish the long orchid paper separately, rather than only as a society paper; the writer asks for candid judgment, not an answer merely to oblige him, and says he will follow it.
evidence: give me your opinion, which I shall implicitly follow
POSSIBLY it might be worth publishing separately
I beg you not to be guided in the least in order to oblige me
probes.loss_to_watch: Changing a request for advice into an instruction to publish.

probes.question: What publishing terms is the writer willing or unwilling to accept?
probes.acceptable_reading: Flexible terms, with half risk/half profit offered as an example, but not publication entirely at his own risk. No agreement has yet been established here.
evidence: I would agree to any terms, such as half risk and half profit, or what you liked; but I would not publish on my sole risk
probes.loss_to_watch: Quoting any terms while losing the sole-risk exception, or treating the example as an agreed contract.

probes.question: Who does the writer think would be interested in the paper?
probes.acceptable_reading: A good many people who care for natural history, but not others; accessibility claims do not imply broad expected demand.
evidence: would interest a good many of such persons who care for Natural History, but no others.
probes.loss_to_watch: Replacing the limited audience expectation with general public appeal.

probes.question: How certain is the writer that separate publication is a good idea?
probes.acceptable_reading: He finds the facts interesting but has great doubts and acknowledges a tendency to overvalue his own work. Not confident commercial success.
evidence: I have myself GREAT doubts on the subject.
I am very apt to think that my geese are swans

probes.question: What final publishing agreement, if any, does this excerpt establish?
probes.acceptable_reading: None is established in this excerpt; it contains a request and possible terms, not the recipient's agreement.
evidence: If I were to publish separately
probes.loss_to_watch: Importing the later publisher reply or background history.

cases.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
cases.edition: Letters to his Family and Friends, Volume I; edited by Sidney Colvin; Methuen, seventh edition, December 1906. Transcribed by David Price; ebook updated 2019-08-25.
cases.locator: Letter to Sidney Colvin, 17 Heriot Road, Edinburgh [January 1875], complete body through signature.
cases.purpose: Explain travel constraints and reconcile wanting company with not imposing a visit; report pending writing plans.
cases.omitted_context: The repeated recipient heading just before the dated letter is excluded; salutation and signature remain. Surrounding letters and editorial material are excluded. Italics markers and punctuation are preserved.

probes.question: What constrains the writer's proposed trip south, and what timing does he suggest?
probes.acceptable_reading: Money appears to prevent it until the session ends at the end of March. This is his tentative assessment, not a booked departure date.
evidence: I think the still small unanswerable voice of coins will make it impossible until the session is over (end of March)
probes.loss_to_watch: Interpreting the metaphor literally or converting a constraint into a confirmed itinerary.

probes.question: How does the writer feel about a visit from Colvin, and what does he ask or expect Colvin to do?
probes.acceptable_reading: He would be very happy to see Colvin but does not want to impose/bother him and resigns himself to a later time. Neither a simple rejection nor an unqualified request to come now captures both sides.
evidence: I do not want you to come and bother yourself
I wish you could come
I see that it is wrong to expect it, and so I resign myself: some time after.
probes.loss_to_watch: Collapsing considerate non-demand into lack of desire, or desire into an obligation.

probes.question: What does the writer say about his father's readiness for a visit?
probes.acceptable_reading: Not quite certain whether his father will be fit for the visitor, though the writer says he now has no real fear about it; preserve the qualification instead of asserting definite fitness or definite illness.
evidence: it is still not quite certain whether my father will be quite fit for you, although I have now no fear of that really.

probes.question: What is the status of the proposal sent to Appleton?
probes.acceptable_reading: The writer offered a series on the modern French school, but has not received an answer; not acceptance or rejection.
evidence: I offered Appleton a series of papers on the modern French school
But he has not deigned to answer my letter.
probes.loss_to_watch: Treating nonresponse as a rejected or accepted proposal.

probes.question: What exact date has been agreed for Colvin's visit?
probes.acceptable_reading: No agreed date is given; some time after is indefinite, and end of March belongs to the writer's possible trip south, not an agreed Colvin visit.
evidence: some time after.
probes.loss_to_watch: Transferring the writer's travel timing to the friend's visit.

deferred: The previous six-source letter/news shortlist remains a scouting record; newspapers, literary scoring and two-hop transmission are deferred.
PG19 title matches for fictional letters and diaries were not treated as evidence of real correspondence.
Austen Letter III and Darwin September 24 were superseded for this pilot by passages with more explicit contingent actions; no model results informed that choice.
